title: The Volunteers Behind the Oxford English Dictionary
text:
In 1857 the Philological Society of London proposed a dictionary that would trace every English word through its history, with quotations showing how each was used over the centuries. No small staff could read enough books to do that. So the project relied on volunteers.

When James Murray, a Scottish schoolmaster and self-taught philologist, became editor in 1879, he issued a new appeal to English speakers across the world. Readers were asked to take books, note words that interested them, and copy each quotation onto a separate slip of paper with the word, the date, the author and the title. The slips poured in by the million. Murray built a corrugated iron shed he called the Scriptorium, lined with pigeonholes to sort them, first at Mill Hill School, where he taught, and later in the garden of his house in Oxford.

The readers were a varied crowd: clergymen, retired officers, housewives, scholars and amateurs. One of the most productive was William Chester Minor, an American former army surgeon confined to Broadmoor asylum after killing a man. From his cell he sent in many thousands of quotations, chosen to fill gaps the editors had listed.

The first section, covering A to Ant, came out in 1884. Murray died in 1915, having reached the letter T. Other editors finished the work, and the complete dictionary was published in 1928.
lesson: Thousands of small, well-organized contributions can build what no expert could build alone. Give volunteers a clear, simple format, and their work adds up.
people: James Murray, William Chester Minor, the volunteer readers
location: Mill Hill and Oxford, United Kingdom
source: K. M. Elisabeth Murray, Caught in the Web of Words (1977); Simon Winchester, The Professor and the Madman (1998)
